prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 alone, with Katori and Ye. Having read all eight first-round statements, I find that the reasons given are consistent and independent of the vote count, and I have tried to check them against my own field instead of against each other. The scientific core is a sharp mechanism: the magic-wavelength condition cancels the differential light shift of the lattice, and Lamb-Dicke confinement then lets a very large number of neutral atoms be interrogated on an ultranarrow transition without Doppler or recoil broadening. That resolves a real conflict between confinement and accuracy, and it is why stability and accuracy improve together. The achievement has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in several national laboratories at about 1e-18, and the hard part, control of blackbody, higher-order light-shift, collisional and density-dependent systematics, is a substantial atomic-structure and many-body result and not only engineering. The credit fits two people and leaves room under the three-person cap. The one change I make in round 2 is to the citation: Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce persuaded me that it should name the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength principle, so that it does not read as a prize for all optical clocks or settle priority among competing laboratories, and I have added that wording. I also now resolve my own round-1 question against bundling ion clocks into this prize, for the reasons below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains novelty margin over the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, which includes ion clocks; a reader could still see the lattice clock as an excellent refinement of a precision-timekeeping story already honoured. I answer it on the physics, but I cannot make the question disappear. The credit is clean for the invention and not for the whole subject, since NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other groups, the ion-clock community and later contributors such as Takamoto are outside the two names. I also still rely on recollection for the early priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and for the relative roles of Katori and Ye; nothing in the supplied record settles it and I do not want my own familiarity with clock physics to stand in for verification. Finally, part of the societal case, the redefinition of the second, is pending, and a precision-measurement prize is a different kind of result from a discovery about nature.

responses.point: Johansson argues against merging lattice and ion clocks, saying the ion line was honoured in 2012 and that adding an ion-clock laureate would turn a clear invention into a broad metrology prize, and she asks that the citation be written around invention and realisation, not a single record number.
responses.response: I accept both points and they change my position. In round 1 I asked whether lattice and ion clocks needed joint recognition; having thought about it, the physical principles differ (single-ion control against many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength), the ion line is already inside the 2012 citation, and a third name from the ion side would blur the boundary without adding an identifiable discovery. I have therefore dropped the joint-recognition idea and reworded my citation around the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping, keeping the 10^-18 figure only as a consequence. I disagree with her only on tone: I would not call the invention independent of Ye's systematic control, so the citation should keep both names tied to invention and realisation together.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B039 to B012 but still calls the Higgs observation the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist and asks whether the redefinition of the second is a precondition for recognition or a confirmation of impact.
responses.response: I treat the redefinition as a confirmation and not as a precondition: the physics of reproduced 1e-18 performance already stands, and I would not want the committee's decision to depend on a metrology-body timetable that is outside the science. I agree with him that B039 is a first-rate result, and I do not rank it below B012 on scientific merit. The reason it is not in my configuration is the attribution problem he himself concedes: Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra are all defensible, and a three-name set is a leadership judgment that I cannot defend as scientific authorship. If the committee finds a principled rule for that choice I would reconsider, but I do not think the supplied record provides one.

responses.point: Kroll says Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and first demonstration are the cleanest anchor for priority, would not bundle ion clocks, names Takamoto and others as contributors outside the credited names, and says my priority caveat should be checked against primary sources before the final ballot.
responses.response: I agree that the priority question must be checked and I want to be explicit that I cannot check it from the supplied files; the chair's first question is right that it is still recollection. I would not treat Takamoto's early strontium work as grounds for adding a third name, because the invention is the magic-wavelength proposal and the demonstration of the scheme, but I would not claim the boundary is verified either. Where I differ from him is on his second choice, B010: Cirac, Zoller, Blatt and Bloch would need a citation that separates the 1995 gate proposal and ion-trap realisation from what the 2012 prize already covers, and with four names that is harder than for the clock.

responses.point: Olsson says a prize should recognise the invention and its demonstrated performance, not wait for an administrative redefinition, and that the strongest consequences (the redefinition of the second, geodesy) are not yet realised.
responses.response: I agree and it is close to my own view, but I would sharpen one point: the consequences that are already realised are not trivial. Clock comparisons at 1e-18, searches for variation of constants and clock-based height measurements are being done now, so the case does not lean mainly on the future. I would, however, resist the argument that the breadth of support from different fields is itself persuasive; Olsson makes this point carefully, and I share it, because the support only counts if the reasons survive scrutiny, which is why I have tried to restate the mechanism in my own terms and to flag what I cannot verify.

uncertainties: Priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and early realisations, and the relative roles of Katori and Ye, which I know from recollection and cannot confirm from the supplied record.
Whether the committee judges the step beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes to be sufficient, which is a matter of weighting that the physics alone does not decide.
Whether other lattice-clock groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Takamoto) make a two-name credit under-inclusive in a way that the citation wording cannot repair.

Whether a collaboration-based discovery (B039, B029) could be credited fairly under the three-person cap; if the committee found a principled rule I would need to reconsider how I rank B012 against them.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my profile documents a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group and Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and work with Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato; none of these people is credited on any shortlisted entry, and nothing in the provided profile ties me to Katori, Ye or any other credited name. I flag only field proximity to precision atomic physics for B012 and B010, and I note, in answer to the chair's fifth question, that I see no disclosed flag of my own that would need a recusal ruling. I have no objection to Johansson stepping back on B051 or Olsson on B021 if either is advanced.
